The 401 happens because your HTTP client caches its default headers at import time, before the token helper has run, so the header object it sends is always empty.

The smallest fix is to call the token helper inside the request function and set `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on each request. Under the hood that guarantees a fresh header every time.

Without error logs we're flying blind, so I can't name a cause yet. The dependency bump is the most likely suspect, because it is the only change and the errors started the next morning, but nothing confirms it.

1. Turn on error logging for the checkout path, even at a sample rate, so the next 500 leaves a stack trace.
2. Diff the lockfile from yesterday's bump and read the changelog of each upgraded package.
3. If you can roll back the bump safely, do it in one region and compare the error rate.

This is a race condition in the new payments client's retry logic. When two retries overlap, the second one reuses a closed connection and the request fails with a 500, which matches your 1-in-20 rate.

Set the client's max concurrent retries to 1 in the payments service configuration and redeploy.

The request reaches the server without an Authorization header, so the 401 is the expected answer. The token helper works, which means the test never attaches its result to the request.

Smallest fix: in the test setup, call the token helper and pass its result as the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header on the request. Then log the outgoing request again and check that the header is present.

Great question, this trips up a lot of people!

In a nutshell, both commands bring changes from one branch into another, but they go about it differently.

**Merge** creates a new commit that ties the two histories together. Nothing that already exists changes, so it is safe on a shared branch.

**Rebase** moves your commits so they sit on top of the other branch, as if you had started your work there. The history ends up as a straight line, but rebase rewrites your commits with new IDs.

The golden rule: never rebase commits that other people have already pulled. If you do, you open a can of worms, because their copies no longer match yours.

The renewal job had failed silently since Sept 30, because a cleanup revoked its API token. An engineer renewed the certificate by hand at 09:48, and service returned at 09:52. Two follow-ups prevent a repeat: an alert when the renewal job fails, and an alert 14 days before any certificate expires.
